column4: Resident of riverine and broad-leaved woodland in northern Botswana.
column5: Mainly large insects, also small birds, rodents and lizards; often hunts by day.
column6: Lays its eggs in a natural hole in a tree.
column7: Told from the Pearl-spotted Owlet by its rounder head and barred (not spotted) back.

column4: Resident of riverine forest and woodland with fruiting trees in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Eats fruit, especially wild figs, picked in the tree canopy.
column6: Builds a flimsy platform of twigs in a tree.
column7: Clambers through branches like a parrot, even hanging upside down, and is hard to see in the leaves.

column3: About 25-30 cm long; the female is much larger than the male.
column4: Resident of wetlands with floating plants such as water lilies.
column5: Feeds mostly on aquatic insects and other invertebrates picked from floating plants.
column6: Polyandrous: the female mates with several males, and each male incubates the eggs on a floating nest.
column7: Very long toes spread its weight so it can walk on lily pads; the male carries chicks under his wings.

column3: About 33 cm long; the smallest duck in southern Africa.
column4: Resident of quiet, clear waters with water lilies, e.g. Okavango, Linyanti and Chobe.
column5: Eats mainly the seeds of water lilies, also other plant parts and small invertebrates.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree, usually close to water.
column7: Despite its name it is not a true goose but a tiny duck; the male has a green and white face.

column4: Resident of shallow wetlands, pans and floodplains; moves around with water levels.
column5: Mostly fish but also invertebrates, caught by sweeping the bill side to side in shallow water.
column6: Builds a stick platform nest in trees or reeds, usually in colonies with herons.
column7: Its spoon-shaped bill is packed with touch receptors, so it can find prey by feel in muddy water.

column4: Common resident of woodland, thickets and riverine bush in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Eats insects and other invertebrates, foraging in groups on or near the ground.
column6: Cooperative breeder with helpers; a host of Levaillant's Cuckoo.
column7: Groups give loud chattering choruses and may fight noisily with neighbouring groups at borders.

column4: Resident of woodland and savannah, solitary or in pairs.
column5: Forages on fallen logs and on the ground for ants and termites, using its sticky tongue.
column6: Nests in a hole excavated in a tree.
column7: Male has red on the head, nape and malar stripe; the female has a brown throat and cheek patch.

column4: Woodland in northern and eastern Botswana; seen mainly in summer.
column5: Eats insects, especially caterpillars, including hairy ones that most birds avoid.
column6: Builds a small, shallow cup nest on a branch, camouflaged with lichen.
column7: Male is all black, often with a yellow patch at the gape; the female looks different, with yellow barring.

column4: Resident of thickets, woodland and bushy savannah, mainly in the north and east.
column5: Eats insects and other invertebrates, mostly hunted on the ground under bushes.
column6: Builds a cup nest low down in a bush or small tree.
column7: Has a loud, slurred whistling song, often given in a display flight above the bush.

column4: Common resident at the edges of rivers, pans, dams and wetlands.
column5: Eats insects, worms and other invertebrates picked from mud and short grass.
column6: Lays well-camouflaged eggs in a scrape on the ground near water.
column7: Named after its metallic 'tink-tink' call, like a hammer on an anvil; boldly dive-bombs intruders.

column4: Uncommon bird of woodland in northern and eastern Botswana; partly migratory.
column5: Eats insects, mainly hunted at night.
column6: Lays 2-3 well-camouflaged eggs on bare ground.
column7: Mostly nocturnal; its large eyes shine in the spotlight on night drives.

column4: Resident of grassland and dry savannah on Kalahari sand; flagship bird of the Central Kalahari IBA.
column5: Feeds almost entirely on seeds; large flocks gather at water-holes in the dry season.
column6: Nests on the ground; parents may walk slowly away to lead predators from the nest.
column7: Males soak their belly feathers at water and fly back to let the chicks drink from them.

column4: Common resident of many habitats, especially savannah and woodland.
column5: Feeds mostly on seeds, occasionally invertebrates; often feeds in flocks.
column6: Builds a flimsy platform nest of twigs, typical of doves.
column7: Its call is often remembered as 'work harder, work harder', one of the commonest sounds in the bush.

column4: Common resident of acacia and broad-leaved woodland.
column5: Eats small insects gleaned from leaves and twigs or caught in short flights.
column6: Builds a tiny, neat cup nest bound with spider web on a branch.
column7: Song sounds like 'three blind mice'; the female has a chestnut chin spot, the male a black breast band.

column4: Palaearctic summer migrant to acacia thornveld and dry scrub.
column5: Eats insects, and also berries before migrating.
column6: Does not breed here; it breeds in Europe and Asia.
column7: This small warbler weighs about 15 g yet flies thousands of kilometres between Europe and Africa.

column4: Resident of woodland, riverine bush and gardens, mainly in eastern and northern Botswana.
column5: Eats mainly insects, often taken on the ground, as well as fruit.
column6: Excavates a nest hole in a dead branch; parasitised by the Lesser Honeyguide.
column7: Its song is a long, steady trill that sounds like an old alarm clock ringing.

column4: Common resident of dry, short grassland and open, bare areas.
column5: Eats insects, especially termites, picked from the ground.
column6: Lays well-camouflaged eggs in a scrape on open ground and defends it noisily.
column7: Named after the white ring around its black cap; it is noisy and often calls at night.

column4: Common summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to woodland, savannah and reedbeds.
column5: Eats insects, especially caterpillars, including hairy ones.
column6: Brood parasite: lays its eggs in the nests of weavers, bishops and sparrows.
column7: Its name comes from its call, a plaintive 'dee-dee-dee-deederik'.

column4: Resident of riverine thickets and woodland in northern Botswana.
column5: Eats insects and other invertebrates found among leaf litter on the ground.
column6: Builds a cup nest in a hole in a tree or stump.
column7: A fine songster with a loud, varied song that often includes imitations of other birds.

column4: Uncommon Palaearctic summer migrant to woodland, mainly in the north and east.
column5: Eats insects, especially caterpillars, and fruit in the tree canopy.
column6: Does not breed here; it breeds in Europe and Asia.
column7: The male is bright yellow with black wings, but it hides in the canopy and is more often heard than seen.

column4: Common resident of woodland and dense savannah, but found in most habitats.
column5: Mostly insects caught in the air; also robs other animals and may take nestlings.
column6: Builds a small, flimsy cup nest in the fork of a horizontal branch.
column7: Mimics meerkat alarm calls so they run for cover, then steals the food they drop.

column4: Resident of shallow water in rivers, floodplains and pans; usually solitary.
column5: Feeds mainly on fish and frogs, with invertebrates a minor part; may feed on moonlit nights.
column6: Nests in colonies, building stick platforms in reedbeds or trees over water.
column7: Our largest white egret; the line of its gape extends behind the eye and its legs are black.

column4: Common resident of woodland, especially mopane, in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Eats insects, fruit and seeds, often foraging on the ground in flocks.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Its glossy blue-green shine comes from feather structure, not pigment; note the dark blue ear patch.

column4: Resident of thornveld thickets and dry savannah.
column5: Eats grass seeds and small insects such as termites, mostly on the ground.
column6: Builds a ball-shaped grass nest; it is the host of the Long-tailed Paradise Whydah.
column7: Also called the Melba Finch; the male has a bright red face and throat.

column4: Uncommon resident of riverine and broad-leaved woodland in northern Botswana.
column5: Gleans small insects from leaves and branches, like a tit.
column6: Nests in a small hole in a tree.
column7: Constantly fans and flicks its tail, showing the white outer tail feathers.

column4: Resident of open grassland, floodplains and pan edges, often near water.
column5: Catches small flying insects in the air, often flying low over the ground.
column6: Nests in a hole in the ground, often an old rodent burrow.
column7: Unusually, it breeds in the dry winter months.

column4: Common resident of dry Kalahari scrub and thornveld; endemic to southern Africa.
column5: Eats insects and other invertebrates hunted on bare ground.
column6: Builds a cup nest low down in a bush.
column7: Often cocks and fans its rufous tail, which has a black and white tip.

column3: About 100 cm long, with a wingspan of about 2.7 m.
column4: Resident of dry savannah and the Kalahari; Critically Endangered, mainly due to poisoning.
column5: Scavenges carcasses, tearing tough skin and sinew; sometimes kills small animals.
column6: Builds a huge stick nest on top of a flat-topped tree and lays a single egg.
column7: Our largest vulture; it dominates other vultures at a carcass.

column3: About 36 cm long, including tail streamers.
column4: Common resident of savannah and dry woodland, solitary or in pairs.
column5: Eats invertebrates and small vertebrates, caught by dropping from a perch.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Rollers are named after their tumbling, rolling display flights; males have slightly longer streamers.

column3: About 45 cm long, including the very long tail.
column4: Resident of acacia savannah in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Eats insects and small vertebrates, dropping on them from a perch.
column6: Breeds cooperatively; builds a cup nest in a thorny tree.
column7: Also called the African Long-tailed Shrike; lives in noisy groups with whistled calls.

column4: Resident of savannah, woodland and riparian forest, in pairs or small flocks of up to 30.
column5: Feeds almost entirely on seeds and fruit, rarely invertebrates.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Like all parrots it has two toes forward and two back, and a powerful bill to crack hard seeds.

column3: Up to about 2 m tall and up to 150 kg; the largest living bird.
column4: Resident of dry, open country, but also savannah and broad-leaved woodland.
column5: Mostly plants; it swallows stones to help grind food in the gizzard.
column6: Several females lay in one ground nest; the black male incubates at night.
column7: The fastest running bird, reaching 95 km/h; it defends itself by kicking with its large toenail.

column3: About 63 cm long and about 2 kg.
column4: Rare resident of tall riverine forest along the Okavango, Linyanti and Chobe rivers.
column5: Catches fish at night, snatching them from the water surface; also frogs.
column6: Nests in a large tree hollow; usually only one chick is raised.
column7: Has bare legs and spiky soles for gripping slippery fish; its call is a deep, booming hoot.

column4: Resident of dry woodland and savannah; fairly common but moves around.
column5: Eats large insects, scorpions and lizards, dropping on them from a perch.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Bulkier than other rollers, with a broad white eyebrow and no tail streamers.

column4: Very common resident of savannah and woodland with grass and bushes.
column5: Eats small insects gleaned from grass and low bushes.
column6: Builds a ball-shaped grass nest low in a grass tuft or bush.
column7: Sings a harsh 'chi-chi-chi-cherrrr' from a bush top; one of the commonest songs in the bush.

column4: Resident of savannah wherever there are large game animals or cattle.
column5: Eats ticks and other parasites from large mammals, and also blood from wounds.
column6: Nests in a tree hole lined with hair plucked from mammals.
column7: Has a yellow ring around the eye; its hissing alarm call warns its host of danger.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to open grassland and savannah.
column5: Catches flying insects in the air, often flying low over grass.
column6: Builds a mud nest with a long entrance tunnel under bridges, culverts or in burrows.
column7: Its dark rufous underparts separate it from the similar Mosque Swallow.

column4: Resident of woodland, especially mopane, in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Eats mainly insects, also some nectar and seeds.
column6: Builds a nest of thin twigs and leaf stalks with an entrance tunnel, hung from a branch.
column7: Unlike most weavers the breeding male has a bright red head, and it weaves with twigs, not grass.

column4: Resident of woodland and savannah, mainly in the north and east.
column5: Catches insects by dropping from a perch, often onto the ground.
column6: Builds a cup nest in a hole, crevice or old nest of another bird.
column7: Looks like a Fork-tailed Drongo but has a square tail, a dark eye and a quieter manner.

column3: About 90 cm long and up to about 4 kg.
column4: Resident of grassland, savannah and open woodland; Vulnerable.
column5: Eats invertebrates and vertebrates up to the size of young hares; groups gang up on large prey.
column6: Cooperative breeder; nests in a large tree hole and usually raises only one chick.
column7: Its deep booming call carries for kilometres; full red face skin only appears at 4-6 years old.

column4: Resident of acacia and mopane savannah.
column5: Eats insects, dropping from a perch to catch them on the ground.
column6: Breeds cooperatively; builds a cup nest in a tree fork.
column7: Lives in noisy family groups, and the helpers assist in raising the chicks.

column3: Up to about 100 cm long; Africa's largest waterfowl.
column4: Resident around lakes, dams and lagoons, avoiding fast water; in pairs or small flocks.
column5: Mostly vegetarian, but will take invertebrates.
column6: Nests on the ground in thick vegetation near water, sometimes in tree holes.
column7: Uses the spurs on its wings to gash enemies; its flesh can be poisonous from eating blister beetles.

column4: Resident of open savannah, solitary or in pairs.
column5: Hunts, pirates kills from other birds and scavenges carrion; prey up to young springbok size.
column6: Builds a stick nest on top of a tree, often an acacia.
column7: Young birds take 3-4 years to reach adult plumage; the female is larger and usually darker.

column4: Resident of riverine thickets in far northern Botswana.
column5: Eats insects and other invertebrates, mostly found low in thick cover.
column6: Builds a shallow cup nest in a thicket.
column7: Pairs sing in a duet so well timed that it sounds like one bird.

column4: Resident of dry acacia thornveld.
column5: Eats grass seeds picked from the ground.
column6: Builds a ball-shaped grass nest; it is the host of the Shaft-tailed Whydah.
column7: Also called the Common Grenadier; the male is rich chestnut with bright violet cheeks.

column4: Resident of open savannah and woodland; Critically Endangered, mainly due to poisoning.
column5: Scavenges carcasses; occasionally steals food or kills prey such as hares and young impala.
column6: Builds a stick nest on top of a tall tree and lays a single egg.
column7: Takes 6 years to reach adult plumage; when threatened it spreads its wings, hissing and snapping.

column4: Common resident of dry acacia savannah.
column5: Eats seeds and insects, foraging on the ground.
column6: Groups build untidy grass nests; roost nests have two entrances, breeding nests one.
column7: Lives in noisy groups, and a single tree may hold many of their straw nests.

column3: About 13 cm long, excluding the tail wires.
column4: Resident near rivers and water in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Catches flying insects in the air, often low over water.
column6: Builds an open mud cup under bridges, rock overhangs or buildings.
column7: Named after the two wire-thin outer tail feathers; it has a bright chestnut cap.

column4: Resident of savannah in northern Botswana where buffalo and other large game occur.
column5: Eats ticks and other parasites, preferring large hosts such as buffalo and giraffe.
column6: Nests in a tree hole lined with hair plucked from mammals.
column7: Its yellow bill with a red tip and its pale rump separate it from the Red-billed Oxpecker.

column4: Common resident of open grassland and floodplains.
column5: Eats small insects gleaned in grass.
column6: Builds a pouch-shaped nest in grass, bound together with spider web.
column7: Its zigzag display flight comes with a sharp 'zit' call at each dip, hence the name.

column4: Summer migrant from tropical Africa to woodland and savanna in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mainly hairy caterpillars and other insects taken in the tree canopy.
column6: Brood parasite; lays its eggs in the nests of the Fork-tailed Drongo.
column7: Its 'hoop-hoop' call sounds like an African Hoopoe, unlike the 'cuck-oo' of the Common Cuckoo.

column3: About 60-65 cm long; the female is larger than the male.
column4: Resident of tall woodland, especially along rivers, in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mostly gamebirds such as francolins and guineafowl, also hares and other small mammals.
column6: Builds a large stick nest high in a tall tree, lined with green leaves; lays 1-2 eggs.
column7: Pairs often hunt together, one bird flushing the prey for its partner.

column4: Resident of riverine woodland in northern Botswana, such as the Okavango and Chobe.
column5: Seeds picked up on the ground.
column6: Builds a flimsy platform nest of twigs in a tree or bush.
column7: Told from the Cape Turtle Dove by its grey head and yellow eye ringed with red skin.

column4: Summer migrant from tropical Africa to woodland and savanna in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects and small lizards caught on the ground from a low perch; it does not need water.
column6: Digs a nest tunnel in an earth bank, the side of an aardvark burrow or a termite mound.
column7: Told from the Malachite Kingfisher by its violet ear patch and lack of a crest.

column4: Summer visitor to flooded grassland and dense marsh vegetation in the Okavango and Chobe.
column5: Plant material and seeds, also insects and snails.
column6: Cup nest of plant stems hidden in reeds or sedges just above the water.
column7: Breeding birds have a bright blue shield on the forehead above the red bill.

column4: Resident of riverine woodland in far northern Botswana, such as the Okavango and Chobe.
column5: Insects caught in short flights from a perch.
column6: Small cup nest placed in a tree hollow, a fork of a branch or an old nest of another bird.
column7: Blue-grey above and paler below, with a short white line above the eye.

column4: Common resident of wetlands with reeds and floating plants, especially in the Okavango and Chobe.
column5: Insects, snails, worms, small fish and frogs found at the water's edge.
column6: Bowl-shaped nest of plant material hidden in reeds or vegetation over water.
column7: Walks on lily pads and has been seen picking parasites off hippos and buffalo.

column4: Resident of woodland and riverine forest in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects picked from leaves and branches in the tree canopy.
column6: Small neat cup nest bound with spider web in the fork of a tree.
column7: The male puffs out his white rump feathers into a fluffy ball when displaying.

column4: Resident of dry acacia thornveld and Kalahari scrub.
column5: Mainly grass seeds taken on or near the ground.
column6: Untidy ball nest of grass with a side entrance, low in a thorny bush.
column7: Easy to know by its black face, grey head and deep red rump and flanks.

column4: Common resident of acacia savanna and woodland, often near water.
column5: Mainly grass seeds, also small insects such as termites.
column6: Ball nest of grass with a side entrance in a thorny tree or bush.
column7: Often builds its nest close to a wasp nest, which helps protect it from predators.

column4: Resident of thornveld and dry woodland with low bushes.
column5: Insects found on or near the ground under bushes.
column6: Neat cup nest placed low in a bush or small tree.
column7: In display it flies up with rattling wings, then glides down giving a falling whistled song.

column3: About 30-34 cm long; the largest glossy starling in the region.
column4: Resident of savanna and open woodland; flocks of 60 or more in late winter and spring.
column5: Mostly insects, also small vertebrates and sometimes berries and flowers.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Will fiercely mob slender mongooses, owls and large snakes.

column4: Resident of woodland and savanna throughout Botswana.
column5: Insect larvae dug out of thin branches and twigs by tapping.
column6: Excavates its own nest hole, usually in a dead branch.
column7: Southern Africa's smallest woodpecker; the male has a red back of the crown, the female black.

column4: Resident of thickets and palm groves in far northern Botswana, such as along the Chobe River.
column5: Insects and other small animals found on the ground.
column6: Cup nest placed in a palm or in a hollow in a tree.
column7: Has a thin black collar around a pale throat and is a good singer that copies other birds.

column4: Resident of reedbeds and papyrus in the Okavango, Linyanti and Chobe wetlands.
column5: Insects, frogs, snails, rodents and small birds.
column6: Builds its own ball-shaped nest of grass and reeds; it is not a brood parasite.
column7: The largest coucal in southern Africa, with a deep bubbling 'doo-doo-doo' call.

column4: Resident of woodland and savanna with thickets in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Seeds, bulbs, berries, insects and termites scratched from the ground.
column6: Lays its eggs in a shallow scrape on the ground under a bush.
column7: Often runs with its tail cocked like a bantam chicken; pairs duet loudly at dawn.

column4: Resident of broad-leaved woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Lizards, rodents, birds and large insects, caught by dropping from a perch.
column6: Stick nest in the fork of a tree, often lined with mud or dung.
column7: Named for its piping song; told from the Pale Chanting Goshawk by its grey, barred rump.

column4: Resident of mopane and other woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Seeds picked up on the ground.
column6: Lays its eggs in a shallow scrape on the bare ground.
column7: Unlike other sandgrouse it comes to drink at dusk, arriving just after sunset.

column4: Common resident around any slow-moving or still water; most often in pairs.
column5: Almost entirely plants such as grass and seeds; insects are eaten by accident.
column6: Nests on the ground, in tree holes, on cliff ledges or on top of old nests of other birds.
column7: Not a true goose; it is related to the shelducks. Females have a thinner neck.

column4: Summer migrant from Europe and Asia; common on passage across Botswana.
column5: Flying insects, especially bees and wasps caught in the air.
column6: Nests in tunnels in sand banks; most breed in Europe and Asia, a few in South Africa and Namibia.
column7: Flocks are often heard calling a soft 'prrrup' high overhead before they are seen.

column3: About 28-36 cm long; the female is larger than the male.
column4: Solitary resident of woodland and savanna, often hunting around water-holes.
column5: Almost only birds caught in flight, doves most of all; it rips open weaver and waxbill nests.
column6: Small stick nest in a tree, often covered with the webs of social spiders.
column7: Young birds take two years to get full adult colours; an all-black form also occurs.

column4: Summer migrant from tropical Africa to savanna and open woodland.
column5: Mainly hairy caterpillars and other large insects.
column6: Brood parasite of crows and starlings; its chick does not throw out the host's eggs or young.
column7: Easy to know by its grey crest, long tail and white-spotted back.

column4: Solitary resident of riverine and broad-leaved woodland, savanna and gardens.
column5: Bee eggs, larvae and wax; also hawks flying insects such as termites.
column6: Brood parasite of hole-nesters like barbets; the chick kills the host chicks with its hooked bill.
column7: Leads people to bees' nests, and can digest beeswax with the help of bacteria in its gut.

column4: Resident of dry savanna, usually in groups of 3-8 but up to 30 birds.
column5: Fruit, flowers, buds and leaves, with some insects.
column6: Flimsy platform nest of sticks in a thorny tree.
column7: Named for its loud 'go-way' alarm call; it mobs large predators and owls.

column4: Resident of thickets and dense undergrowth in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Small insects found in low, dense bushes.
column6: Builds a nest inside living leaves that it sews together with spider web.
column7: Its call is a loud bleat like a lamb, which gave it the old name 'Bleating Warbler'.

column4: Resident wherever there is shallow water; usually alone or in pairs.
column5: Mostly frogs and tadpoles; fish and insects are less important.
column6: Builds a huge domed nest of sticks and mud with a side entrance, often used later by owls and geese.
column7: The name is Afrikaans for 'hammer-head', after the shape of its head and crest.

column3: About 105-135 cm long; males can weigh more than 12 kg.
column4: Resident of dry open savanna and grassland, alone or in loose groups.
column5: Mostly insects, also small vertebrates and carrion.
column6: Lays 1-2 eggs on bare ground; the male displays by puffing out his white neck feathers.
column7: One of the heaviest flying birds in the world; the flagship bird of the Kgalagadi park.

column4: Summer migrant (some stay all year) in northern and eastern Botswana, often near buildings.
column5: Flying insects caught in the air.
column6: Builds a bowl-shaped mud nest with an entrance tunnel under bridges, eaves or rock ledges.
column7: Told from the Greater Striped Swallow by its heavy black streaks and orange head.

column4: Common resident of woodland and thornveld throughout Botswana.
column5: Small insects picked from branches and bark.
column6: Hanging purse-shaped nest of grass and spider web below a twig.
column7: It has almost no tail, so it looks like a small round ball creeping along branches.

column4: Common resident of acacia savanna, especially in the Kalahari.
column5: Insects caught by dropping onto the ground from a low perch.
column6: Small cup nest in the fork of a thorny tree.
column7: Named after the Marico district in South Africa; brown above and clean white below.

column4: Nomadic; arrives in woodland and grassy savanna in the north and east after good rains.
column5: Seeds and insects taken on the ground.
column6: Cup nest on the ground next to a grass tuft.
column7: Males repeat the same short song over and over, day and night, which gives the bird its name.

column4: Resident of savanna with palm trees, usually in pairs or flocks.
column5: Small insects caught in the air.
column6: Glues a small pad of feathers to the underside of a palm frond with its saliva.
column7: It glues its eggs to the hanging nest so they do not fall out in the wind.

column3: About 25-28 cm long, not counting the male's pennants.
column4: Summer migrant to broad-leaved woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Flying insects such as moths and beetles caught at dusk and night.
column6: Lays its eggs on bare ground among leaf litter, with no nest.
column7: Breeding males grow long white wing pennants, up to twice the length of the body.

column4: Resident of riverine woodland in northern Botswana, such as the Okavango and Chobe.
column5: Nectar, small insects and spiders.
column6: Small hanging oval nest with a side entrance, decorated with lichen and bark.
column7: Told from the similar Marico Sunbird by its smaller size and shorter bill.

column4: Resident of dry acacia savanna, often near large trees such as baobabs.
column5: Seeds and insects, mostly taken on the ground, often near game.
column6: Groups build large untidy nests of thorny twigs in big trees; males have several females.
column7: Males have an unusual false penis, a feature found in very few other birds.

column4: Nomadic; moves in huge flocks through savanna and thornveld, following seed supply.
column5: Grass seeds and grain.
column6: Breeds in colonies of up to millions, with small woven ball nests in thorn trees.
column7: Thought to be the most numerous wild bird on Earth, with over a billion birds.

column4: Common resident of Kalahari thornveld and dry woodland.
column5: Insects such as termites and beetles, also seeds and fruit.
column6: Lays its eggs on bare ground with no nest.
column7: In display the male flies straight up, then tumbles down as if shot and opens his wings at the last moment.

column4: Resident of broad-leaved woodland, such as mopane, in northern Botswana.
column5: Insects and caterpillars found in the tree canopy.
column6: Cup nest on a branch; group members help feed the chicks. Host of the Thick-billed Cuckoo.
column7: Lives in groups that move through the trees together; note the red bill and eye ring.

column4: Resident of woodland and savanna in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects and their larvae picked from bark and leaves.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree; other group members may help feed the chicks.
column7: The male is glossy black with white wing markings; it often joins mixed bird parties.

column4: Common resident of savanna and dry scrub; forms large flocks, especially when breeding.
column5: Seeds, insects and nectar.
column6: The male weaves ball nests with the entrance below; one male has several females.
column7: Breeding males are bright yellow with a black mask and red eye, and mob predators.

column4: Resident of acacia savanna and dry woodland.
column5: Rodents, small birds, insects and scorpions.
column6: Uses old stick nests of other birds or a hollow in a tree.
column7: When afraid it can make itself very thin and upright, or puff up to look much bigger.

column4: Resident of woodland and savanna; it does not need water.
column5: Insects and small lizards caught on the ground from a perch.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree, often an old barbet or woodpecker hole.
column7: When calling it opens its wings to flash the white underwings.

column4: Common resident of rank grass and thickets, especially near water.
column5: Small insects found in grass and low bushes.
column6: Ball nest of grass woven into living leaves; may be parasitised by the Cuckoo Finch.
column7: Often holds its long tail cocked up and waves it while scolding loudly.

column3: About 58-66 cm long; the largest owl in Africa.
column4: Resident of dry savanna, woodland and riverine woodland, usually in pairs.
column5: Small to medium mammals and birds, even young vervet monkeys and warthog piglets.
column6: Lays its eggs in old stick nests of other birds, such as eagles or Hamerkops.
column7: Has bright pink eyelids, easy to see when it blinks.

column4: Resident of river banks and wetlands, in pairs or family groups.
column5: Insects and other invertebrates, and small vertebrates.
column6: Scrape on the ground near water; it will attack predators with open wings to defend the nest.
column7: Often nests close to nesting crocodiles; its sad whistle is heard at night.

column4: Resident of tall broad-leaved woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Caterpillars and other insects in the tree canopy.
column6: Shallow cup nest of lichen and spider web on a horizontal branch.
column7: A quiet grey and white bird of the treetops that is easy to overlook.

column4: Resident of lakes, dams and lagoons; groups of about 40, but flocks of thousands occur.
column5: Mostly plant matter, also invertebrates.
column6: Nest on the ground in grass or reeds near water.
column7: A whistling duck: its three-note whistle is often heard at night as flocks fly over.

column4: Summer migrant from Europe and Asia to shallow pans and flooded grassland; usually alone.
column5: Mostly invertebrates, also small frogs and fish.
column6: Breeds in northern Europe and Asia, sometimes using old songbird nests in trees.
column7: When flushed it flies off calling a shrill 'chiff-iff-iff'.

column4: Resident of woodland and thickets in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Small insects gleaned from leaves.
column6: Ball-shaped nest of plant down, moss and spider web with a side entrance.
column7: Pairs sing duets; the male usually has a small black bar on its yellow breast.

column3: About 63–73 cm long; the female is larger than the male.
column4: Common resident of rivers, lakes and floodplains such as the Okavango, Chobe and Linyanti.
column5: Mostly fish, but also birds up to flamingo size, monitor lizards, young crocodiles and even vervet monkeys.
column6: Builds a large stick nest in a tall tree near water and often reuses it for many years.
column7: Young birds are untidy and blotchy; full adult colours only appear by the fifth year.

column4: Resident of woodland and gardens, usually seen alone or in pairs.
column5: Small invertebrates caught by probing its long bill into the ground.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree or wall; the nest has a foul smell that may help keep predators away.
column7: Named after its soft 'hoop-hoop' call; it raises its crest like a fan when alarmed or landing.

column4: Resident around shallow water and slow-moving rivers, common in the Okavango; alone or in large flocks.
column5: Mostly water snails, plus freshwater mussels which it may leave in the sun to open.
column6: Builds a stick platform nest in trees or reedbeds, usually in colonies with other waterbirds.
column7: The gap between the closed mandibles develops with age; young birds have a closed bill.

column3: About 15–17 cm long; the smallest owl in southern Africa.
column4: Widespread resident of dry woodland and savanna, including mopane and acacia.
column5: Mainly large insects such as moths, beetles and grasshoppers, plus spiders and scorpions.
column6: Lays its eggs in a natural tree hole without adding nest material.
column7: By day it stretches tall with ear tufts raised to look like a broken branch; its call is a soft 'prrrup'.

column4: Resident of mature mopane woodland in northern Botswana, usually in pairs.
column5: Insects, mostly caught on the ground by dropping from a low perch.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree, often an old barbet or woodpecker hole.
column7: The male is black with a white cap; the female is black with a white throat and breast.

column3: About 23–25 cm long; one of the largest woodpeckers in the region.
column4: Resident of mature woodland with big trees, including mopane and riverine forest.
column5: Mainly beetle larvae dug out of dead wood with its strong chisel-like bill.
column6: Excavates a nest hole in a dead branch or trunk.
column7: It drums very loudly on dead wood, and the sound carries a long way; note the bold black 'beard' stripe.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to woodland and riverine forest in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mainly hairy caterpillars, which most other birds avoid.
column6: Brood parasite that lays its eggs mainly in the nests of boubous and other bush-shrikes.
column7: Its mournful three-note call is often remembered as 'I'm so siiick'.

column4: Resident of woodland, riverine forest and gardens in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mainly fruit, especially figs, with some insects.
column6: Excavates a nest hole in a dead branch; extra group members often help raise the chicks.
column7: Pairs sing a loud duet ('too-puddly') to declare their territory as they patrol its borders.

column4: Summer visitor from Europe and Asia to floodplains and pans, often in large flocks, e.g. at Lake Ngami.
column5: Insects, especially grasshoppers and locusts, caught in flight and on the ground.
column6: Does not breed in Botswana; it breeds in eastern Europe and central Asia.
column7: Near Threatened because of heavy pesticide use on its breeding grounds; flagship bird of the Lake Ngami IBA.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to riverine forest and tall woodland in northern Botswana.
column5: Flying insects, especially swarming termites, caught in the air.
column6: Nests in a natural hole high in a tall tree.
column7: Most active in the late afternoon, when it gorges on emerging flying termites.

column4: Common resident of acacia and broad-leaved woodland across Botswana.
column5: Insects gleaned from leaves and twigs in the tree canopy.
column6: Builds a small, neat cup nest in a fork, bound with spider web and covered in lichen.
column7: The male's call is a long trilling 'prrrrrr', like a telephone ringing; the female often answers.

column4: Resident of acacia woodland and savanna, usually in small groups.
column5: Small insects gleaned from leaves in the tree canopy.
column6: Builds a small cup nest in a tree.
column7: Named for the narrow brown band across its throat, which looks like a burn mark.

column4: Nomadic in dry, open grassland and bare ground, often near pans; usually in flocks.
column5: Seeds and some insects picked up from the ground.
column6: Small cup nest on the ground next to a grass tuft or stone, often after rain.
column7: The male is boldly black and chestnut with a white cheek; it was formerly called a finchlark.

column4: Found on open floodplains, sandbanks and pan edges in northern Botswana; numbers change with water levels.
column5: Insects caught in flight like a swallow, mostly at dawn and dusk.
column6: Lays eggs in a bare scrape on open ground, usually in loose colonies.
column7: With its forked tail and pointed wings it flies like a large swallow; it fakes injury to lure intruders away.

column3: About 20–25 cm long; the smallest francolin in the region.
column4: Resident of grassland and open woodland on sandy soils in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Seeds, shoots and insects found on the ground.
column6: Nests in a scrape on the ground, lined with grass and hidden in cover.
column7: Its name comes from the call, a repeated 'ko-kwee, ko-kwee'.

column4: Common resident of acacia thornveld, especially in the Kalahari.
column5: Mainly insects, mostly taken on or near the ground.
column6: Builds a cup nest of bark strips in a fork of a thorn tree.
column7: Pairs sing a fast duet; rarely, birds have a yellow instead of a crimson breast.

column4: Common resident of riverine woodland, thickets and gardens in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Fruit, nectar and insects.
column6: Builds a thin cup nest in a bush or tree; it is a host of the Jacobin Cuckoo.
column7: Often the first bird to give a scolding alarm at a snake or owl; it bathes by shaking in wet leaves.

column4: Summer visitor from further north in Africa to open woodland, bare ground and burnt areas.
column5: Insects picked from the ground.
column6: Does not breed in Botswana; it breeds further north in central Africa.
column7: Looks like a small Groundscraper Thrush and flicks its wings up after landing.

column4: Common resident of woodland and thickets in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Seeds picked up from the ground.
column6: Builds a flimsy platform nest of twigs in a bush or low tree.
column7: Its sad, descending 'du du du-du-du-du' call is often told as 'my mother is dead, my father is dead...'.

column4: Resident of Kalahari sandveld with grass and scattered bushes.
column5: Insects and seeds taken on the ground.
column6: Cup nest on the ground at the base of a grass tuft or small bush.
column7: Unlike many larks it often sings from the top of a bush; note its white eyebrow.

column4: Resident of woodland and riverine forest across northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Ants and beetle larvae taken from bark and dead wood.
column6: Excavates a nest hole in a tree branch.
column7: Gives a loud, nasal 'wheeeaa' call; the tail feather shafts are golden-yellow.

column3: About 140–180 cm long; weighs about 7–12 kg.
column4: Resident but nomadic on large open water; the flooded Makgadikgadi Pans hold huge breeding colonies.
column5: Only fish, with up to 4 kg recorded; it scoops fish into its throat pouch.
column6: Breeds in dense colonies on the ground, such as on islands in the Makgadikgadi when flooded.
column7: Flocks feed together, herding fish into shallows, which is more successful than feeding alone.

column4: Resident of broad-leaved woodland and riverine trees in northern Botswana.
column5: Small insects gleaned from leaves in the tree canopy.
column6: Builds a small cup nest in a tree.
column7: Moves through the canopy in small, chattering groups, often in mixed bird parties.

column3: About 8–9 cm long; one of the smallest birds in Africa.
column4: Resident of acacia savanna and dry woodland, including the Kalahari.
column5: Tiny insects and their eggs gleaned from leaves and twigs.
column6: Builds a soft felt nest of plant down with a false entrance; the real entrance is a spout that closes.
column7: The fake entrance leads to a dead-end pocket, fooling snakes and other nest robbers.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to woodland and savanna in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mainly insects such as grasshoppers, and small lizards; it seldom eats fish.
column6: Digs a nest tunnel into a river bank or earth bank.
column7: A dry-land kingfisher, recognised by its grey head, chestnut belly and red bill.

column3: About 53–58 cm long; weighs about 1.3 kg.
column4: Common resident of savanna and grassland; in pairs when breeding, otherwise in flocks.
column5: Mainly plant material and arthropods.
column6: Lays a large clutch in a scrape on the ground hidden in grass.
column7: Gives a fast 'kek kek kek krrrr' alarm for raptors and cats, so it is a useful predator alarm.

column4: Resident and nomadic in grassland and open savanna across Botswana.
column5: Seeds and small insects found on the ground.
column6: The female mates with several males (polyandry); the male incubates the eggs and raises the chicks.
column7: Not a true quail; the larger, brighter female makes a deep hooting call to attract males.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to savanna, woodland and riverine forest.
column5: Mostly caterpillars; often joins mixed feeding flocks.
column6: Brood parasite of babblers, which raise the cuckoo chick.
column7: Its chick is raised by a whole group of babblers, and it begs with calls like a babbler chick.

column3: About 34 cm long, about half of which is tail.
column4: Resident of mopane and riverine woodland in northern Botswana, e.g. along the Chobe.
column5: Insects taken on the ground, plus some fruit.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: Formerly called the Long-tailed Starling; its long, graduated tail makes it easy to identify.

column4: Resident of acacia and riverine thickets in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects gleaned from leaves in the tree canopy.
column6: Builds a flimsy, shallow cup nest in a tree or bush.
column7: Heard far more than seen; its call is a whistled 'poo-poo-poo-pooooo'.

column3: About 18–19 cm long; weighs about 80 g.
column4: Common resident of woodland and savanna across Botswana.
column5: Insects, small birds, rodents and lizards; it often hunts by day.
column6: Nests in a tree hole, often an old barbet or woodpecker hole.
column7: Two dark 'false eyes' on the back of its head make predators think it is watching them.

column4: Common resident of slow-flowing or still open water, in pairs or close family groups.
column5: Mostly small fish, plus insects and crustaceans.
column6: Digs a nest tunnel into a river bank; helpers often assist the breeding pair.
column7: Hovers over water before diving; males have two breast bands, females one broken band.

column3: About 36 cm long, including the tail.
column4: Uncommon resident of mature broad-leaved woodland in northern Botswana.
column5: Insects, often caught by dropping from a perch to the ground.
column6: Nests in a natural hole in a tree.
column7: The two outer tail feathers end in small 'rackets'; it is quiet and easily overlooked.

column4: Common resident of thickets and gardens near water in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Small grass seeds picked up from the ground.
column6: Builds a ball-shaped grass nest with a side entrance; host of the Village Indigobird.
column7: The indigobird chick is raised alongside the firefinch chicks without harming them.

column4: Common resident of dry savanna and woodland, in pairs or coveys of up to 12.
column5: Mainly seeds and arthropods.
column6: Nests in a scrape on the ground under a bush or grass tuft.
column7: One of the best 'predator alarms' in Botswana: its loud 'KAK! KAK! KAK!' warns of cats, snakes and raptors.

column4: Resident of reeds and rank vegetation near water in northern Botswana.
column5: Insects gleaned from low vegetation.
column6: Builds a ball-shaped nest low down in rank grass or bushes.
column7: Has a rusty face and gives a loud, ringing whistled song from cover near water.

column4: Resident of savanna and woodland with thickets, alone or in pairs.
column5: Invertebrates and small vertebrates; it may scavenge on fish carcasses.
column6: Builds an untidy ball-shaped nest of grass in a thicket.
column7: Its bubbling 'doo-doo-doo' call sounds like water being poured from a bottle.

column3: About 33–38 cm long, including the tail streamers.
column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to savanna, grassland and river banks; very sociable.
column5: Almost only flying insects caught in the air.
column6: Breeds in large colonies, digging nest tunnels into river banks or flat ground.
column7: Follows game-drive vehicles and animal herds to catch the insects they disturb.

column4: Common resident of mopane and dry woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Mainly insects such as beetles and termites, mostly found on the ground.
column6: The female seals herself into a tree hole and moults all her feathers while she incubates.
column7: Feeds on the ground more than most hornbills; the male feeds the sealed-in female through a slit.

column4: Common resident of dry, open savanna and woodland, in pairs or small family groups.
column5: Invertebrates and small vertebrates such as snakes, lizards and rodents, plus seeds and fruit.
column6: The female seals herself into a tree hole and moults all her feathers while she incubates.
column7: Gives a 'krrrrr' call when a predator is near and will fly over and circle above it.

column4: Resident of open grassland and savanna, in pairs or small family groups.
column5: Mainly plant material and arthropods.
column6: Nests in a scrape on the ground hidden in grass.
column7: Has red bare skin on the face and throat; males call loudly at dawn and dusk from a mound or log.

column4: Resident and nomadic on short grassland, bare ground and recently burnt areas.
column5: Insects picked up from the ground.
column6: Lays its eggs directly on bare ground, often on burnt veld.
column7: Quickly arrives at freshly burnt areas; it runs, stops suddenly, then runs again.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to woodland and riverine forest in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Fruit and insects.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree, lined with leaves.
column7: The male is shining violet and white; the female is brown and streaked, so they look like different birds.

column3: About 120–130 cm tall; the largest crane in Africa.
column4: Resident of shallow floodplains; the Okavango Delta holds a key population. Vulnerable.
column5: Mostly plant matter, plus snails, frogs and fish in shallow flooded areas.
column6: Builds a mound nest in shallow marsh and usually lays only one egg.
column7: Will follow a leopard or other predator, calling 'kwarrrr' repeatedly; flagship bird of the Okavango IBA.

column4: Resident of riverine thickets and gardens in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects and other invertebrates found on or near the ground.
column6: Builds a cup nest in a hollow stump or bank; pairs stay together for one season.
column7: Its loud song rises in volume, repeating phrases faster and faster, often at dawn.

column3: About 78–85 cm long; weighs about 4–5 kg.
column4: Uncommon resident of savanna and woodland, usually alone or in pairs.
column5: Carrion, often arriving first at small carcasses; it also kills small animals.
column6: Builds a stick nest on top of a tall tree and lays one egg.
column7: Critically Endangered due to poisoning; the female has white inner wing feathers, the male grey.

column4: Summer visitor (intra-African migrant) to woodland and riverine trees in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Insects and small lizards caught from a perch; it seldom eats fish.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree, often an old barbet or woodpecker hole.
column7: Its loud trill 'trrp-trrrrrrrrr', with wings spread open, announces that summer has arrived.

column4: Resident of mopane and broad-leaved woodland in northern and eastern Botswana.
column5: Seeds and insects.
column6: Nests in a hole in a tree.
column7: The small yellow throat spot is hard to see; look for the pale eyebrow instead.
